prompt.context: Your client is a mobile service provider in an Asian country. They were targeting the high and medium segments in the country. Recently they acquired another service provider which targeted the lower segment of the market. The two companies had two different brands before, and they kept both brands after the merger.
prompt.question: To the CEO's surprise, the overall pre-tax profit has been lower than the combined pre-tax profit of the two companies when they were not merged. You are hired to figure out why and how we can improve that.

framework: Use the profitability formula: Profit = (P - VC) * Volume - FC
Consider product mix: two brands (H brand targeting high/medium segments, L brand targeting lower segments)
Cost has been optimized post-merger — investigate revenue side
Break revenue into Price x Volume x Mix by brand and sub-segment

questions.prompt: Has pricing changed for either brand after the merger?
questions.guidance: Pricing plans for both H brand and L brand did not change. However, actual revenue received per customer per month has been flat on H brand and decreasing on L brand. Candidate should probe into why revenue per customer is falling on L brand despite no pricing plan change.

questions.prompt: Why is revenue per customer on the L brand decreasing even though the pricing plan did not change?
questions.guidance: L brand targets two sub-segments: LM (middle income) and LL (low income). Volume is flat overall, but the mix within L brand has been shifting toward LL (lower-priced sub-segment), which is pulling down average revenue per customer. Volume and pricing per plan are unchanged; it is purely a mix effect.

questions.prompt: What caused the mix shift within L brand toward the LL sub-segment?
questions.guidance: The company heavily promoted the LL sub-segment plan, successfully attracting more LL customers. However, this promotion did not cause cannibalization within L brand sub-segments, nor between H brand and L brand. The likely cause is that competitors reacted — possibly by targeting the LM sub-segment, causing LM customers to churn to competitors while LL grew. Candidate should identify this as a competitor-driven dynamic.

questions.prompt: How would you verify whether a competitor took LM customers away?
questions.guidance: Review the historical customer database to identify churned LM customers. Conduct targeted exit surveys asking: (1) Why did you leave? (2) Which provider did you switch to and why? These two steps are the practical verification approach.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the possible reasons the customer mix within L brand shifted toward the lower-income sub-segment (LL)?

categories.name: Internal / Company Actions
ideas: Company heavily promoted the LL plan, attracting more low-income customers
Marketing spend and messaging skewed toward LL, making it more visible

categories.name: Competitor Actions
ideas: Competitor targeted the LM sub-segment with aggressive offers, poaching LM customers
Competitor launched a plan specifically priced to undercut the LM tier

categories.name: Customer Demand Shift
ideas: Macro economic change caused middle-income customers to downgrade or churn
Market maturation in LM segment led to natural migration

categories.name: Product / Pricing Design
ideas: LL plan over-delivered value relative to LM, causing internal upgrade/downgrade confusion
Lack of differentiation between LM and LL plans made LM unattractive

recommendation: The profit decline is driven by a mix shift within the L brand: promotional activity on the LL sub-segment grew that tier, while the higher-revenue LM sub-segment appears to have lost customers — most likely to a competitor
To restore profitability, investigate and stem LM customer churn, and reassess whether the LL promotion is creating net value given the revenue dilution effect
risks: If competitors continue targeting LM customers, defensive measures may require price reductions that further compress margins
Aggressive LL promotion may signal a race to the bottom in the lower segment
next_steps: Analyze historical customer database to quantify LM churn rate and identify when it began
Conduct exit surveys of churned LM customers to confirm competitor poaching
Evaluate whether the LL promotional spend generates sufficient volume to offset the revenue-per-customer decline
Consider whether LM plan pricing or features need to be refreshed to retain that sub-segment
